analysis.one_liner: Stops new mountaintop removal coal mining permits until a federal health study is finished.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred to three House committees, having drawn 15 Democratic sponsors and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would freeze new federal permits and permit renewals for mountaintop removal coal mining — blasting off mountaintops with explosives in Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Virginia — until federal health scientists complete a study of whether that mining is making nearby residents sick. Existing mines could keep operating but would have to continuously monitor and publicly report water, air, noise, and soil pollution. The federal cost of the study and monitoring would be paid by a one-time fee on companies that conduct or conducted this kind of mining.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities near mountaintop removal mines in the four Appalachian states covered by the bill. The bill's own findings cite peer-reviewed research associating this mining with elevated rates of birth defects, chronic lung and heart disease, lung cancer, and mortality in surrounding counties [S3]. The moratorium would block any new or expanded mining authorization until a National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences study concludes there are no health risks [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Appalachian communities near mountaintop removal mines

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Army, EPA, Interior, or states from issuing or renewing federal permits for mountaintop removal mining, or expansions of existing projects, until the Secretary of Health and Human Services publishes a determination that the mining poses no health risk to nearby residents.

Requires companies operating these mines to continuously monitor water, air, and noise pollution and regularly monitor soil pollution, and to report results monthly to HHS, which must post them in a searchable public database within 7 days.

Directs the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to conduct a comprehensive study of health impacts on people living near these mines and make the results public, with a one-time fee on current and past mining operators covering the federal cost.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that practice mountaintop removal mining. They would pay a one-time fee for the study and monitoring program, bear the cost of continuous pollution monitoring, and be unable to obtain new or renewed permits — or expand existing mines — until the health study concludes their operations are safe.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets no deadline for the health study, so the moratorium on new permits and renewals could last indefinitely while the study proceeds, and permit renewals for existing operations are also frozen under the same standard.

Coal mining remains a significant employer in parts of Appalachian Kentucky, West Virginia, and Virginia, and an open-ended permitting freeze would affect jobs and tax bases in counties with few alternative employers — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.
Existing mines could continue operating throughout, so the bill would not stop pollution from current operations; it would only impose monitoring and reporting on them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 440,000-plus residents of counties where mountaintop removal is practiced, the bill offered a way to find out whether a documented pattern of elevated birth defects and chronic disease is linked to the mining next door, at a cost charged to the mining companies rather than taxpayers [S3]. The main honest objection is the open-ended freeze: without a study deadline, it functions as a long-term halt on new mining, which carries real economic weight in coal-dependent counties. The bill could have addressed that with a deadline; it did not.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees in July 2023, but no committee ever held a hearing or voted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Morgan McGarvey (D-KY) introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, joined by eight original co-sponsors, all Democrats.
The Speaker referred it to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure committees; within a day it was sent to two subcommittees.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies holding existing mountaintop removal operations kept working with no new monitoring or reporting requirements, and no federal study of the health effects was ever funded. Residents near the mines got neither the moratorium nor the data.

for.name: Morgan McGarvey

for.name: 14 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill; all co-sponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: As chair of the lead committee, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or vote appears in the record.

against.name: Coal mining industry
against.role: Operators of mountaintop removal mines in Appalachia
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed permitting moratoria on mountaintop removal mining.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican co-sponsored the bill; Republicans held the House majority and the three committees of referral, where the bill received no action.

industries.note: The bill would freeze their new and renewed permits pending a health study, charge them a fee for the study, and require continuous pollution monitoring with public reporting of results. Their interest in continuing to mine without these conditions runs against the interest of nearby residents in knowing whether the mining is making them sick.

industries.industry: Eastern Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, and Tennessee coal communities
industries.note: Residents near the mines would gain the health study and public pollution data, but mining jobs and local tax revenue tied to existing operations could be affected by a permitting freeze that has no deadline.
